name: Organizing HOA Decisions for Seismic Retrofits in Los Angeles County Condos

mainEntity.name: How can Los Angeles County condo HOAs organize decision-making and cost-sharing for mandated seismic retrofits in multi-owner buildings?
mainEntity.text: How can Los Angeles County condo HOAs organize decision-making and cost-sharing for mandated seismic retrofits in multi-owner buildings?

acceptedAnswer.text: In Los Angeles County, condominium associations confronted with mandated seismic retrofits face complex governance and cost-sharing challenges. Unlike single-owner buildings, decisions require collective agreement among multiple unit owners with varying financial capabilities and risk tolerance. The HOA board should begin by reviewing governing documents to understand requirements for approving major capital projects and special assessments. Some CC&Rs specify voting thresholds, notice periods, and assessment formulas that must be followed. Next, commission a building-wide structural evaluation and conceptual retrofit plan from an engineer experienced with local ordinances. This report should outline options, estimated cost ranges, and likely construction impacts. Boards can then host informational meetings where the engineer explains risks, ordinance deadlines, and potential consequences of inaction. Financing strategies may include special assessments, reserve reallocations, or HOA-level loans repaid through increased dues. Allocations are often based on ownership percentage or unit factors defined in the CC&Rs, but boards may need legal guidance if certain units benefit more or are affected differently. Clear, transparent communication and phased decision-making—concept approval, budget approval, contractor selection, financing approval—can improve owner buy-in. Documenting meeting minutes, votes, and professional recommendations helps demonstrate diligence and maintain compliance with governance requirements.
acceptedAnswer.description: Condo HOAs in Los Angeles County facing seismic retrofits must align governing documents, voting thresholds, and assessment powers. Boards should commission a master evaluation, communicate cost ranges, obtain legal and engineering guidance, and structure special assessments or loans that equitably allocate retrofit costs among unit owners.
